summary: Defines semantics that let an HTTP client and server do byte-range GET and HEAD requests starting at any offset and ending at an unknown offset, for content that keeps growing over time. This is an experimental approach for live or appending content.

eli5.summary: If a video keeps being recorded, you may want to start watching from any point and keep going as it grows. This lets web requests do that.

questions: how to stream appending content over http
subtitle: HTTP range requests that start at any byte and continue indefinitely as new content is appended, for streaming and live data.

tldr.problem: Live or continuously appending content (video streams, logs, blockchain data) has unknown length. Clients either download from the beginning (inefficient) or poll repeatedly for new bytes (high latency). Existing HTTP range requests do not work because servers do not know when a client wants an open-ended response.
tldr.mechanism: A client signals support by sending a byte-range request with a very large end position, much larger than the expected content size. A server that supports this responds with a Content-Range header that echoes that exact large end position, signaling an indefinite-length response that continues as content is appended.
tldr.outcome: Clients can now efficiently start reading from any point in growing content and continue indefinitely, receiving new bytes as the content is appended. Servers that do not support it respond normally (with the current available range), so clients can fall back gracefully.

today: RFC 8673 is Experimental. It enables efficient streaming of live and appending content using standard HTTP range request mechanisms. No standardization path is guaranteed, but the approach is designed to be compatible with existing HTTP implementations.

sections.title: Live Content and Range Requests
sections.content:
HTTP range requests (via the Range header) let clients request a byte range of a representation. This is useful for resuming interrupted downloads or seeking within video. However, standard range requests assume the representation has a known, fixed length. Live content (live video or audio streams, continuously appended logs) does not: bytes are added over time and the total length is unknown.

Clients need to access live content efficiently. They might want to start at a specific byte (e.g., a video keyframe before the live point) and continue reading as content is appended. Existing HTTP mechanisms do not handle this: full downloads are inefficient, and polling with periodic range requests introduces latency or overhead.
sections.eli5: Imagine reading a book that is still being written. You want to start at chapter 5 and keep reading as new chapters arrive, not start from chapter 1 every time.

sections.title: Establishing the Random-Access Range
sections.content:
This RFC proposes a two-step process. First, a client sends a HEAD request with an open-ended range (e.g., Range: bytes=0-) to discover what bytes are currently available and whether the content is appending. The server responds with a Content-Range header that specifies the available byte range with an asterisk in place of the total length, indicating the length is unknown.

For example, a HEAD request might return Content-Range: bytes 0-1234567/*, indicating bytes 0 through 1234567 are accessible, but the total length is unknown. This tells the client that the server has live content and what range can be accessed immediately. The client can then decide to start reading from the live point or from an earlier point.
sections.eli5: First, you ask 'how many chapters are done so far?' The server says 'chapters 1 through 50, and more are coming'. Now you know where to start reading.

sections.title: Open-Ended Range Requests
sections.content:
Once the client knows the content is live, it can request a range with a very large end position. For instance, a client might send Range: bytes=1230000-999999999999, where the end position is much larger than the content size. A server that understands this protocol echoes that large end position in the Content-Range response: Content-Range: bytes 1230000-999999999999/*. This signals to the client that the response will continue indefinitely, streaming new bytes as they are appended.

A server that does not support this feature simply returns the currently available range, as it would for any range request. For example, it might return Content-Range: bytes 1230000-1234567/*, ending at the current end of the content. Clients must be prepared to handle both: supporting servers echo the large end position, non-supporting servers return the current end.

The server should use chunked transfer coding and not provide a Content-Length header for indefinite-length responses. The connection continues until the content source ends or a 0-length chunk is sent.
sections.eli5: You ask for bytes one million to one billion. The server that understands this says 'okay, I will send from one million indefinitely' by echoing one billion. A server that does not understand just sends up to what it has and stops.

sections.title: Use Cases and Compatibility
sections.content:
This mechanism enables efficient access to several types of live content. A client can request a range starting from a video keyframe near the live point and stream indefinitely for low-latency live video playback. A shift-buffer resource (like a time-shift recording that discards old content at the front) can be accessed by first querying the current random-access range, then requesting from any point within it with an indefinite end. Long-lived log files and blockchain data can be accessed the same way.

The RFC stresses compatibility: servers and intermediaries that do not support this feature are unaffected. A client that does not recognize the indefinite-length response falls back to polling or other mechanisms. Caching proxies can cache responses to ranged GET requests because the Content-Range header specifies what portion is in the response.

For shift-buffer representations, GET requests without a Range header should not be cached, because the first byte can change. Servers should use redirect responses or Cache-Control headers to prevent unintended caching.
sections.eli5: New and old systems work together. If a server does not get it, the client tries something else. Everyone stays compatible.

sections.title: Implementation and Security
sections.content:
The RFC recommends using 2^53-1 (9007199254740991) as the large end position unless an application needs a different value. This is the largest integer safely represented in JavaScript and is sufficient for long-duration, high-bitrate streams. Some applications may need larger values.

A security concern is that servers must handle large byte-position values without integer overflow. The simplest approach is to store and return the end position as a string rather than converting it to a number, avoiding overflow bugs. Servers must also check that the requested range is satisfiable before consuming resources.
sections.eli5: Use a big number for the end position. Make sure your code does not break when it sees a very big number.
